gh-1426124038.title: GitHub - NoRain211/doa2u-re: Native Windows port of Dead or Alive 2 Ultimate (Xbox), built by static recompilation with a hand-written runtime. Requires your own copy of the game.
gh-1426124038.content:
A native Windows, macOS and Linux port of Dead or Alive 2 Ultimate (Xbox), built by static recompilation, with the goal of rewriting it into readable source.

Download ·
Features ·
Bring-up notes ·
Report a bug
Sister projects: DOA3 ·
DOAXBV

ImportantThis project ships no game files. You need your own legally obtained copy
of Dead or Alive Ultimate (Xbox, USA), Disc 2. It is not affiliated with or
endorsed by the game's rights holders.

About
The DOA2 game executable on Ultimate's second disc is lifted to C with a
static recompiler, then linked against a hand-written runtime that replaces
the Xbox kernel imports and the game's Direct3D 8, DirectSound and input
libraries (XDK build 5849) with native Windows equivalents: Direct3D 11 or
Vulkan, XAudio2 and SDL3. On macOS and Linux the same runtime renders through SDL_GPU
(Metal or Vulkan) and plays through SDL3 audio. The rest of the game still runs
as generated code. The plan
is to replace game logic with readable, hand-written source while the game
keeps running.
Features

The whole game, recompiled. Boot, menus, character select, Story,
Watch and the attract demo run on the original game code, lifted to C.
macOS and Linux. Native Metal and Vulkan builds through SDL_GPU, for
Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, Linux PCs and the Steam Deck, from the same
lifted program and HLSL shaders as Windows. A gamepad settings screen works
in Steam Game Mode. See building on macOS and Linux.
Native renderer. Direct3D 11, or Vulkan through SDL_GPU, at 480p to 4K, the game's own 16:9
widescreen camera and menus (the 3D view also widened to 16:10, ultrawide or 32:9, the HUD and menus kept 16:9), MSAA up to 32x (8x on Vulkan) and SMAA Ultra. Water
reflections render at the output resolution; bloom and lighting follow the
game's own passes.
Xbox-like pacing. Frames flip on the next refresh as on the Xbox, at
60 fps, including heavy rain-stage fights at 4K. On Windows, VRR: On is
for G-SYNC or FreeSync displays and tears on fixed-refresh ones; it is not
yet verified on a VRR monitor.
Audio and movies. Music and voices through XAudio2, with 3D voices
through the game's HRTF tables and I3DL2 reverb, in stereo or the game's
own 5.1 surround mix. The intro and story movies play.
Controllers. Xbox, PlayStation and other SDL3 controllers, and the
keyboard for player 1.
Free camera. Take the game's camera in fights and cutscenes and fly it
anywhere, freeze the scene, hide the HUD and save screenshots. Turn it on in
the launcher; see free camera.
Launcher. Launcher.exe picks resolution, anti-aliasing, widescreen, the
renderer, VRR, an optional intro-movie skip, 5.1 surround, the unlock
setting, random CPU costumes, the free camera and the staff-roll dedication
card, and remembers them. DOA2U.exe plays with the same choices. On release
ZIPs after 0.1.10, the settings launcher on each platform can check GitHub
for a newer release and install it from its UPDATE page; Check At
Start turns the start-up check off.
PC Settings in the game. The game's own Options menu has a
PC SETTINGS row after Video, drawn and translated like the game's
rows, with the launcher's settings. Unlocks, CPU Costumes,
Free Camera and Dedication change at once, and with the Vulkan
renderer so do Resolution, MSAA and SMAA; the others say they
apply the next time the game starts. Leaving the page saves them for the
launcher too.
Quit Game. The main menu ends with a QUIT GAME entry, lettered and
drawn like the game's own, that asks before it closes the game.
Sharper menus. The Vulkan renderer redraws the game's 2D art (menus,
fonts, the HUD) at four times its size with xBRZ the first time each piece is
shown, so it stays smooth at high resolutions. RECOMP_UI_UPSCALE=0 turns
it off.
Saves. Your profile and unlocks save to private\play-disc; every
character and costume is offered unless you choose Earn on the
launcher's GAMEPLAY page. Your profile only ever saves what you have
earned, so choosing Earn later gives it back as it was. The game's soft reset
(Start + Back + both triggers) restarts it.
Built from your disc. Launcher.exe lifts the game from your ISO and
refuses any executable other than the one the developers tested.

Status
Warning0.3.2 Alpha is bring-up software. Story, Watch and the attract demo play
in development runs on every stage, but many modes and characters have not
been tried. A draw the port cannot render yet stops the game with a message
in the log.

Area
State

Boot, menus, attract demo, character select
Working

Stages
Every stage played

Story endings
Every ending, its credits and epilogue play

Story, Ayane and Gen Fu
Stages 1-6 cleared without a stop in scripted runs; the Tengu fight was lost each time

Watch
Fights played, including Kasumi vs Lei Fang on The Burai Zenin at 4K and 60 fps

Other characters, Versus, Tag, Survival, Time Attack, Sparring
Not yet played through

Tengu's stage, The Miyama
In Stage Select, before Random, outside Tag; played in Sparring only, other modes not yet played through

Every character and costume
Unlocked by default (the launcher's Earn option leaves them to play); profiles save only what was earned

Native 16:9 widescreen, 16:10, ultrawide and 32:9, up to 4K, MSAA up to 32x, SMAA Ultra
Working, chosen in the launcher; 32:9 tried only in the attract demo and Story character select, on Direct3D 11 and Vulkan

Vulkan renderer on Windows
Working, chosen in the launcher; not yet tested on AMD; MSAA stops at 8x; VRR is Direct3D 11 only

Audio, including 3D voices and reverb
Working

Intro and story movies
Play; the launcher can skip the intro ones

Xbox and other SDL3 controllers, keyboard
Working; keyboard drives player 1

Free camera, scene freeze, screenshots
Working in the attract demo on macOS; a frozen stage's leaves and branches still move

Xbox Live menus
Report no account; Yes quits to the desktop in place of the Dashboard

Online Versus
Rollback netplay from the Versus menu; test build

Hand-written game logic
Not started; the game runs as generated code

macOS and Linux
Boot, menus and the attract demo render at 60 fps through Metal and Vulkan, with MSAA up to 8x and SMAA (building)

Known issues: a demanding moment on The Burai Zenin can still drop a
single frame; the safari stage's heat haze does not ripple yet, and its water
leaves a gap between the elephants' reflections. The game's bloom glows
around bright surfaces as on the Xbox, which reads more strongly on a sharp
4K image.
Play the alpha
On macOS and Linux, including the Steam Deck, follow
building on macOS and Linux instead.
Requirements: Windows 10/11 x64, internet access for the first build, and
your Disc 2 ISO with about 6 GB free. The ZIP carries Python (with Capstone and
Pillow) and CMake, so there is nothing to install.
The build downloads the pinned llvm-mingw
compiler (190 MB) into tools\llvm-mingw and checks its SHA-256; it needs no
Visual Studio or administrator approval.

Download the ZIP from the
latest release and
extract it into a new folder with a short path, such as C:\DOA2U.
Open Launcher.exe and drag your Disc 2 ISO onto it (or choose it on the
BUILD GAME page); the build starts at once. Wait for Build complete
(about 10 minutes). The build stops unless it reproduces the exact program
the developers tested.
Pick resolution, MSAA, SMAA, widescreen, the renderer and VRR on VIDEO SETTINGS, stereo or
5.1 on AUDIO SETTINGS, the intro skip on MOVIES and Earn on
GAMEPLAY to leave unlocks to play, then choose
START GAME. A controller, the keyboard or the mouse all work. Your
choices are remembered, and DOA2U.exe plays with them later.

The first launch copies about 700 MB of the game's disc archives into its
hard-disk cache, which takes a few seconds. Saves and the cache
live in private\play-disc. The package contains tools and source, never a
prebuilt runner or game data. GitHub's automatic source archives lack the
pinned lifter and extractor; use the release ZIP.
Controls: the first connected controller, or the keyboard for player 1:
arrows are the D-pad, Enter is Start, Backspace is Back, Z/X are A/B, A/S are
X/Y, Q/W are White/Black and E/R are the triggers. F3 turns on, or off again,
a readout of the frame rate, the average frame time and the slowest frame of
the last second; it starts off. F11 or Alt+Enter switches between a window and
borderless fullscreen.
To rebind the keyboard, create private/keyboard.json with the buttons to
change, for example {"a": "Space", "b": "Ctrl", "start": "Tab"}. Buttons are
up, down, left, right, start, back, a, b, x, y, white, black, ltrig and rtrig;
keys are A-Z, 0-9, F1-F9, F12, Up, Down, Left, Right, Enter, Backspace,
Space, Tab, Shift, Ctrl and Esc. Buttons you leave out keep their keys,
except that a key you give to one button leaves the button that had it. F10
is a Windows system key, and F11 and Alt+Enter are reserved for fullscreen, so
none of them can be bound. F3 keeps its
readout and, with the free camera turned on, F1, F12 and P keep their jobs,
so a button bound to one of those does both. The free camera's own keys stay
fixed, and while it flies the keyboard is the camera's.
Offline, hold Back for two seconds to quit to the desktop: A quits, B keeps
playing.
Build from source
The public tests need no game files or lifter checkout:
git clone https://github.com/NoRain211/doa2u-re.git
cd doa2u-re
python -m unittest discover -s tools -p "test_*.py"
python tools/public_export.py verify --require-public-tree
cmake -S recomp-runtime -B build/recomp-runtime
cmake --build build/recomp-runtime --config Debug
ctest --test-dir build/recomp-runtime -C Debug --output-on-failure
To also test real PCM consumption on this PC's audio endpoint, configure with
-DRECOMP_NATIVE_AUDIO_TEST=ON. Passing tests does not establish game
compatibility.
To build the game from a clone, initialize the lifter and pass your ISO:
git submodule update --init tools/xboxrecomp
python tools/package_test.py --launchers .
python tools/build_game.py <your-disc-2.iso>
python tools/run_game.py --play
The importer extracts the disc once into private/imported-disc with XboxDev
extract-xiso (on PATH, or bundled
in the release ZIP), selects the game executable by its SHA-256 and leaves
the ISO unchanged. Only that hash is published, in tools/build_game.py.
A different ISO is staged first and replaces that extraction and receipt only if it verifies; a wrong disc keeps the previous import.
After a runtime change, python tools/build_game.py --build-only reuses the
authenticated lift; --lift-only generates without building. Generated C,
receipts and logs stay in private/.
The lift reads the committed function list in tools/doa2u/functions;
--disassemble rebuilds that list from the executable (about 25 minutes)
after a change to tools/doa2u/seed_functions.json or the lifter pin.
tools/doa2u/function_status.json is the decompilation registry. It records
the Ghidra name for each tracked function and, once it is more than a name,
its status (named, decompiled, bound or tested). A bound or tested
entry also names the host source and symbol; the runtime replacement stays
in recomp-runtime/program_manual.c or the adapter's own manual lookup. Raw
decompiler output, generated C and retail bytes stay under private/.

Statuses are exclusive; progress counts decompiled, bound and tested. The
exporter rewrites this table from function_status.json after each refresh.
The initial decompiled entries are the named functions that already carry a
Ghidra comment; the rest stay named until their bodies are worked through.
python -m unittest discover -s tools -p "test_*.py" checks every registry
address against the committed function list and checks bound symbols exist.
Refresh names and tags with tools/doa2u/ghidra/ExportFunctionStatus.py from
Ghidra's Script Manager against DOA2.xbe; add that folder to Ghidra's script
directories or load it through GhidrAssistMCP. It keeps existing statuses and
accepts the registry path as its first argument. Names outside
tools/doa2u/functions are skipped and reported; add those addresses to
seed_functions.json and regenerate the list first.
run_game.py takes the launcher's settings as switches, and
--seconds <n> runs a bounded probe instead of --play:
python tools/run_game.py --play --resolution 2160 --widescreen --msaa 32 --smaa
python tools/run_game.py --play --no-widescreen --msaa 1 --no-smaa
python tools/run_game.py --play --resolution 1440 --screen 3440:1440
The game picks its own 16:9 camera and menu layouts from the dashboard video
setting, and the presenter shows that image at 16:9.
--screen W:H (RECOMP_D3D_WIDESCREEN=W:H), from 4:3 to 4:1, keeps that
widescreen mode in another shape: the runner widens the game's projection to
it, so the 3D view fills the screen at the same height, and the presenter
keeps the 16:9 HUD and menus in their shape in the screen's center. The
launcher's 16:10, Ultrawide (the primary monitor's own shape) and
32:9 choices set it. Online sessions and replays use the host's 4:3 or
16:9 mode, fitted with black bars, as both sides must compute the same
frames. Above 480p the Direct3D 11 window fills the screen borderless in
any shape, with black bars around a picture of another shape; the SDL_GPU
window is resizable and fits the picture the same way. MSAA resolves before
SMAA, and gamma applies last; unsupported MSAA counts fall back to the
highest count the GPU supports. Options passed to run_game.py bypass the settings
window. The build fetches pinned, hash-verified copies of SDL3,
upstream SMAA and
Dear ImGui, which draws the free camera's panel.
At first launch run_game.py builds an image from
private/dedication-photo.jpg (shipped in the release ZIP) with Pillow.
Choose Dedication: Hide on the launcher's GAMEPLAY page or the game's
PC SETTINGS page, or pass --no-dedication-card to run_game.py, to skip it.
--no-unlock-all, or Unlocks: Earn on the launcher's GAMEPLAY page, turns
off the automatic character and costume unlock, so unlocks come from play.
With the unlock on, saves and the game's awards still keep to what each
profile earned, so turning it off gives the profile back with its own
unlocks. Profiles saved by builds before this change keep the unlocks those
builds saved.
--random-cpu-costumes, or CPU Costumes: Random on the GAMEPLAY page,
dresses CPU opponents in Story, Time Attack, Survival and Team in random
unlocked costumes where the game would give their first one. Story's special
picks, such as a costume about to unlock, stay. It stays off online.
To package a release ZIP from a clean checkout:
python tools/package_test.py 0.3.2-Alpha
python tools/package_test.py 0.3.2-Alpha --platform macos
python tools/package_test.py 0.3.2-Alpha --platform linux
It zips the files of committed HEAD that building and playing on that platform
need, the pinned lifter's lift and licenses, and the photo from
private/release-assets/. The Windows launchers embed private/launcher-icon.ico,
and packaging stops without it. Developer notes, tests outside the build and other
platforms' launchers and backends stay out; tools/package_test.py lists them.
The Windows ZIP adds extract-xiso and its license
with test-release.md as README.txt; the macOS and
Linux ZIPs use test-release-macos.md and
test-release-linux.md.
Repository layout

Path
Contents

recomp-runtime/
Runtime, kernel and input adapters, audio, D3D8 replacements, D3D11 and SDL_GPU presenters, tests

xbe/
XBE parsing and hashing

tools/
Disc import, build, launcher, packaging and export checks; pinned lifter submodule

docs/
Bring-up notes, reuse provenance, decisions and the release README

private/
Ignored local game inputs, generated output and run evidence

Contributing
Translation defects are fixed in the
lifter and regenerated; generated
game C is never patched by hand. Read bring-up and
reuse before changing an adapter.
When reporting a bug, say
what you did and what happened, and copy the recomp stop or crash lines
from the end of the newest log in private\play-logs (or the error from the
newest private\build-logs folder). Logs show your home folder and user name
as ~; remove any other private paths, and never upload
game binaries, generated game C, assets, extracted filenames, saves or whole
logs.
AI assistance
This project uses large language models and AI coding agents extensively for
code, reverse-engineering analysis, debugging, tests and documentation. Their
output can contain mistakes; changes are reviewed and tested, and unverified
behavior is tracked as such.
License
Original code and documentation are licensed under
GPL-3.0-or-later; see also NOTICE. Third-party components
keep their own licenses. The license grants no rights to the game or its assets.

gh-1400563069.title: GitHub - kirklandsig/halo2-decompiled: Halo 2 decompilation (decomp) for the original Xbox: a matching decompilation of the retail game into C/C++ source, rebuilt byte for byte, toward native PC, Linux and handheld ports. Contributors welcome. Source only; bring your own disc.
gh-1400563069.content:
Halo 2 Decompilation (work in progress)
Halo 2 Decompilation is an independent preservation and reverse-engineering
project. It studies the retail executable of Halo 2 for the original Xbox
and recreates its program logic in human-readable C and C++ through
independent analysis. Each recreated function is checked against the retail
executable: built with the period-correct compiler, it must produce exactly
the same bytes. That check is what makes the recreated code verifiable. A
longer-term research goal is to study how the game's code could run on other
platforms, using game data that each user supplies from their own copy.
Alongside the game's own code, the project also decompiles Havok, the
physics library linked into the game, because Halo 2's vehicles, ragdolls and
projectiles have to behave exactly as they do on the Xbox. The executable's
other libraries (the Xbox SDK's, Bink video and so on) are not decompiled; a
port would replace them.
The project is non-commercial and is not affiliated with or endorsed by
Microsoft, Bungie or 343 Industries. Read LEGAL.md for the
project's scope, what it does not contain, and its rules for contributions,
and PROVENANCE.md for where its information comes from.
This is a community-driven decompilation. It is built in the open by many
people: contributors who claim a range and send pull requests, and maintainers
who review, merge and keep the build honest. Many of the people working on it,
the maintainer included, work alongside AI coding agents such as Claude and
Codex, and every change still has to pass the same byte-for-byte check and
review. Everyone who has helped is credited in
The community.
Contributors are welcome. No prior decompilation experience is needed,
only patience and some C. New here? Start with
docs/START_HERE.md: the setup checklist, how to claim
a range, and a prompt you can paste into an AI coding agent. Then see
How to help and CONTRIBUTING.md.
What this repository does not contain

Halo 2 game assets: maps, textures, models, audio or cinematics.
The game executable (XBE) or a disc image.
Microsoft Xbox SDK/XDK files: the compiler, libraries or headers.
Havok SDK material: headers, documentation, samples or source. The
Havok code here is recreated from the retail executable and named by what it
does.
Original or leaked Halo 2 source code.
Leaked symbols, PDBs or linker maps. Names that came from such sources
through a third-party dataset have been removed from the inventory, and
names in the source that matched such sources have been renamed; see
PROVENANCE.md.
Confidential or internal Microsoft, Bungie or 343 Industries material.

Requirements
To build or check anything, you must supply any original game files you need
from a copy of Halo 2 that you are legally entitled to use. The project does
not provide game files.
The project does not distribute the Microsoft Xbox SDK/XDK or any proprietary
Microsoft development tools. Contributors are responsible for ensuring that
any development tools they use are obtained and used lawfully. The
maintainers cannot provide, link to, or assist with obtaining proprietary
SDK/XDK materials. Byte-for-byte checking currently depends on the original
compiler, and no open-source toolchain can reproduce its output yet.
Analysis, documentation and review do not need it.
Status
Decompilation is under way, and 10616 retail functions now match byte for
byte. The checker reports:
matched 10616 of 11326 game functions (2032419 of 2786206 bytes, 72.95%)
matched 1345 of 1436 Havok functions (198690 of 290362 bytes, 68.43%)
matched 11994 of 17654 functions in scope (2235534 of 3904218 bytes, 57.26%)

Matched code so far includes:

the script engine's built-in functions;
AI, actor behaviours and actor slot handlers;
object damage, shields and vitality;
network sessions, message codecs and the bitstream;
UI screens and widgets, and the game engines;
sound sources, looping sounds and Bink movie playback;
the game's data arrays, object lists and hash tables;
geometry, quaternion and matrix maths;
input, file paths, localized strings, random numbers and game state;
most of the Havok physics library's functions, from collision agents and
constraints to ragdolls and file streams.

Every function is checked automatically on every build, so a match stays a
match. Refer to docs/PROGRESS.md, which is updated as work
lands.
The target
The retail disc build of Halo 2, as found on the retail disc:

default.xbe SHA-256
03215919bb7163259257d361f4c7bf802a7ab12aa85e2689436369b5c427935d

Internal name
halo2ship.exe

Linked
2004-09-28

Xbox SDK
XDK 5849 (libraries 1.0.5849)

Compiler
Visual C++ 7.1 from XDK 5849 (cl 13.10.3077), /GL /Gr with /O2 or /O1 per file, linked with /LTCG

The approach
The aim is a matching decompilation: C source that the original compiler
turns back into the same bytes as the retail XBE. Matching gives every
function an automatic pass or fail, and that check is what made the Halo CE
decompilation dependable.
Halo 2's retail build is harder than Halo CE's. It was compiled with
link-time code generation (LTCG): the compiler generates code for the
whole program at once, when it is linked. So functions are inlined across
source files, and internal functions get custom calling conventions. 42.5%
of the functions called in the retail XBE take arguments in eax, ebx,
esi or edi, which MSVC's standard conventions never do. Under LTCG, a
function's bytes depend on its callers and callees, not only on its own
source. We know of no earlier project that has matched such a build.
So the work runs in stages:

Feasibility spike (done). Rebuild retail functions with the XDK 5849
compiler in LTCG mode, and find out whether their bytes can be matched.
They can: custom calling conventions, deleted arguments and inlining
decisions all reproduce. The test sources are in spike/.
Project set-up (done). The function inventory, the build with each
source file's flags, the checker and the ready queue.
Decompilation (in progress), from the leaf functions up. What has
worked best on this build, such as fixing a callee's calling convention so
its callers match, and the pitfalls (aligned locals, link order), is
collected in docs/DECOMPILING.md.
Readability (in progress, alongside 3). Once a group of functions
matches, it gets names from what the code does, structs for the data it
reads, and a source file named after its subsystem, without changing a byte
of the build.
Havok (in progress, alongside 3). The physics library is decompiled the
same way. It was a prebuilt library compiled without LTCG, so it matches
with plain per-file flags; see
docs/DECOMPILING.md.
Native port. The game and Havok code from stages 3 and 5, with the Xbox
SDK, Bink and the other libraries replaced.

Build and check

Install the Python dependencies: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt.

Point the tools at your local files. The retail XBE from your own copy
goes at orig/default.xbe (or set RETAIL_XBE), and the development
toolchain's xbox folder at sdk/xbox (or set XDK_DIR); see
Requirements. Both folders are git-ignored and must never
be committed. In Git Bash, also run export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, which
stops Git Bash rewriting the /-style arguments (such as /O2) that the
compiler takes. To read the XBE out of a disc image of your own copy:
python tools/xiso_extract.py "Halo 2.iso" orig default.xbe

The inventory, config/functions.csv, is already committed, so you don't
need to regenerate it. Its name column holds only library functions'
names, from their signatures in the SDK libraries; its object column is
empty. See PROVENANCE.md.

Run python tools/check.py. It builds the whole game as one LTCG image,
compares every decompiled function with the retail bytes, and writes each
function's status (matched, near or todo) back to
config/functions.csv. It exits 1 while any function differs.

Pick work with python tools/ready.py, following
docs/DECOMPILING.md. --claims takes a saved copy
of the Active claims
table so the list skips ranges someone already has.

Tool
Use

tools/xiso_extract.py
Lists or extracts the files of an Xbox disc image.

tools/xbe.py
Summarises an XBE: sections, linked libraries, certificate.

tools/ltcg_probe.py
Counts the functions that take arguments in registers (the LTCG evidence above). Needs capstone.

tools/inventory.py
Finds every function in the XBE and writes config/functions.csv, naming library functions by their signatures.

tools/functions.py
Function discovery that the inventory uses.

tools/libsig.py
Recognises library code by byte signature from the SDK's .lib files.

tools/build.py
Builds the whole game as one LTCG image, with each source file's flags.

tools/check.py
Compares our functions with retail and records progress. Needs the SDK and capstone.

tools/ready.py
Lists the functions that are ready to decompile next. --claims drops addresses from a saved copy of the Active claims table; --owner third:havok lists Havok functions instead of the game's.

tools/open_work.py
Lists work a contributor can claim (source files with functions left, and functions ready to write) outside every person's claim, with the claim line to use. Takes a saved copy of issue #9.

tools/permute.py
Searches variants of a source function for ones that turn a near-miss into a match.

tools/near.py
Counts the near-misses in the csv by source file (functions, bytes). No XBE. --list prints each function.

tools/masked.py
Lists what check.py cannot see because it masks address fields: float constants one step away from the source's literals, strings, and script function definitions that differ from retail. Needs the retail XBE and capstone.

tools/disasm.py
Disassembles retail code.

tools/match.py
The spike's one-file matcher, kept for reference. Replaced by check.py.

How to help
Halo 2 has about 11,300 game functions, so there is room for many people.
docs/START_HERE.md walks through these steps and has a
ready-made prompt for AI coding agents.

Get set up as in Build and check, with your own
lawfully owned copy of Halo 2 (see Requirements).
Pick a source file or an address range that no other person holds (the
pinned Active claims
issue lists claims; the maintainers' automated lanes make way for
contributors), and open a draft pull request saying what you are taking.
python tools/open_work.py lists what is open.
Decompile, run python tools/check.py, and push as functions match.
docs/DECOMPILING.md explains the conventions and
the compiler's quirks.

Havok functions are open too, and a gentler start than the game's: no
whole-program optimisation, so they match with plain per-file flags.
python tools/ready.py --owner third:havok lists the ready ones; claim a
range the same way.
Not ready to write code? Analysis helps too: several contributors have
mapped a function or a subsystem in a docs/ note that the next person then
decompiled.
Details are in CONTRIBUTING.md, including the
contribution provenance policy.
Questions are welcome as issues.
The community
Thank you to everyone who has contributed to this project so far:

@Banshee64, the first contributor: input,
team allegiances, Bink playback, looping sounds, damage, projectiles, unit
actions, vehicles, path search, cloth, recorded animations and devices, and
then the match-tuning of all of it.
@coldspear: matches across the game, among
them object damage and its owner, online tasks and the upload connection,
and big score cuts in dozens of near misses; much of the tooling (the
permuter's mutations, masked.py, the near-miss report, claim-aware
ready.py, the ByteMatch report (then decomp.dev) and the hardening of the disc and XBE
readers); and analysis documents for the object core, weapons, surface
lighting, Havok, the Xbox Live logon and more.
@BirchWoodGod: matched ranges all over
the game, from units and bipeds to network voice, team balancing, map paths,
animation channels and lights, analysis of the network channel and session
search code, and the published analysis credited below.
@BrassMonkey71: matched functions in the
unit and biped code, AI and elsewhere.
@mjshfrvstj-sys: the CI that runs the
Python tests on every pull request, and disc-image tests.
@mrv777: an analysis of the capture the flag and
assault objects.
@RWayne93: online messages, a documented
near miss, and the match of 0x119280, the creature death timer.
@andrewnakas: the inventory fixes that
took WMADEC's data tables and the DSOUND, XNET and D3D section tails out of
the function list, and dozens of fixes checked against retail in the render
state, sound, AI and camera code, including disabled drafts brought to
compile and behave as retail.
@Roasted-Codes: the first contributor
matches in Havok, the physics library: its collision-pair dispatch and
collision agents, constraint serialization, motion steps, and the
library's file streams and string helpers.
@ccgman123: a careful diagnosis of seven
near misses, the cleanup that removed an in-body pragma from 0x9d1c0, the
match of 0x1f3230, and the tools that keep disabled drafts out of the ready
and open-work lists.
@marioag0412: matches across the game,
starting with 0x1e3480 (an object's actor index) and taking in the global
preferences, network voice, online tasks and AI code, big score cuts in
render and tag-function code, and notes on what still differs in a dozen
near misses.
@averycpawelek: matches in the unit
code and nearby (0xc7100, 0xe5840, 0xe2d80 and more) and near misses
brought closer, then much of Havok: its constraint helpers, ragdoll and
hinge descriptions, service lifecycle and stream helpers, and shared
physics helpers.

@kirklandsig maintains the project: runs the
build, reviews and merges every pull request, and keeps the
Active claims
table. Much of the maintainer's own decompilation runs in automated lanes
driven by Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI): AI coding agents that
write and tune the source under the same checks and provenance rules as
everyone else, with each batch reviewed before it lands. Many contributors use
the same tools. The techniques in docs/DECOMPILING.md
were worked out by all of them, people and agents alike, and the commit
history credits each change to its author.
Want to be on this list? See How to help.
Credits

halo-symbol-atlas
(CC BY 4.0): the name and object columns of config/functions.csv once
came from this dataset. Because its names for this build derive from linker
maps of unreleased builds, that data has been removed. See
PROVENANCE.md.
punpckhdq/halo,
bnunu/halo-1 and
halo-ce-universal:
the Halo CE decompilation and port that this project follows. punpckhdq/halo
is AGPL-3.0 since 2026-10-17 (CC0 before); its AGPL revisions are read for
understanding only, never copied from (see PROVENANCE.md).
BirchWoodGod/halo2-decomp:
a functional recovery of the same XBE. Its published analysis gave us
leads: the subsystem lifecycle table, the data-array layout and some
register conventions. We verified each one against the retail code
ourselves; none of its code or text is used here.
Project Cartographer and
H2Codez (GPL-3.0): their
documented Halo 2 Vista tag definitions gave us tag layouts and field names,
which come from the publicly released Halo 2 Vista Editing Kit. We verify
each layout against the retail Xbox code and write our own declarations;
none of their code or text is copied.

LEGAL.md.

The community list them.

gh-1396842451.content:
Chupathingy
Halo CE: Ported for Everyone.

In testing

Community ports

Download ·
chupathingy.org ·
Games online now ·
Discord

Play Halo: Combat Evolved on your PC, Mac, Steam Deck or phone. Campaign, split screen, System Link, and online games with players on every platform.
It plays like the Xbox game. Everything extra is a setting.
You need your own copy of the game. Chupathingy never includes or downloads Microsoft's files.
New: Halo MCC maps
Own Halo: The Master Chief Collection on Steam? Its Halo CE Workshop maps now play in Chupathingy, on Windows, Mac and Linux.

Browse the Workshop in the Delta Guide, with each item's picture and page.
Link Steam once by scanning a QR code with the Steam app. The game never sees your Steam password.
Maps download straight from Steam, with no Steam client needed. Once they're in, they play offline or online.
MCC maps show in every map screen, with search, next to your Xbox and PC maps.
Host and join MCC games, on your own machine or a dedicated server.

How it works, and what you need: docs/mcc.md.

Get it
Download the latest release from the Releases page.

System
Download

Windows 10 or later
chupathingyce-windows64-release.zip

Mac, Apple silicon or Intel
chupathingyce-macos-release.zip

Linux
chupathingyce-linux64-release.AppImage

SteamOS
chupathingyce-linux64-release.AppImage

Android 9 or later, 64-bit
chupathingyce-android64-release.zip

FreeBSD
chupathingyce-freebsd64-release.zip

Step-by-step setup for each system, including the Steam Deck, is in docs/install.md. Older 32-bit PCs and the Linux zip are there too.
The game checks for updates when it starts and asks before installing one. It only installs updates we've signed. On a Mac, it opens the download page instead.
First start on Windows. If Windows warns about an unknown publisher, choose More info, then Run anyway.
First start on a Mac. Move ChupathingyCE to Applications and open it. If macOS won't open it, go to System Settings > Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway. You only do this once.
Set it up

Start Chupathingy.
Pick your Halo: Combat Evolved disc image (.iso or .xiso) from the original Xbox. Any region works.
Wait while it copies the maps (about 2 GB). Then you're in.

Have Halo PC or Custom Edition? The same screen takes the Halo PC disc and the Custom Edition installer too. See docs/maps.md.
On Android, copy the disc image to your phone first.
Where your maps, settings and saves go: docs/install.md.

Join a game. Open Multiplayer > Online Games, pick a game and press A. Or press Join on stats.chupathingy.org.
Host a game. In Online Games, press Y to create one. Everyone can see it on the list.
Invite a friend. Send them your game's invite link.
Play the campaign together. Host it online from Create Game. Here's how.

Chupathingy players on every platform play together. Compatible with OpenCE build-355 (network version 44) for online play: their players can join your games, and you can join theirs.
Friends can't get into your game? See docs/online.md.

Features
Playing together

An Online Games list in the Multiplayer menu
Our servers around the clock, plus the community's
Split screen for up to four, and System Link with no internet or account
Online co-op through the campaign
Friends, parties and clans in the Delta Guide (F3), with party links you can paste in Discord
Text and voice chat, and host tools to kick or ban

Maps

Every Xbox map from your disc
Halo PC, Custom Edition, HaloMD and MCC Workshop maps, side by side with the Xbox ones
Missing maps download when you join, and each one is checked before it's used
Community Xbox map packs, like Halo CE+
Stubbs the Zombie, an early work in progress, from your own Xbox maps (off by default)

Your stats

A carnage report with medals for every finished game
Service records and leaderboards on stats.chupathingy.org
Your Delta profile, right in the game

How it looks and feels

The Xbox menus, with Halo PC's settings added
High-res HUD and text, and widescreen
Controller layouts, Bumper Jumper included, with button prompts for Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo pads
5.1 and 7.1 surround, and a headphone 3D mode
The intro and cutscene movies from your disc

Every setting, and the config.toml file behind them: docs/settings.md. What each platform has: docs/builds.md.
Consoles
Chupathingy also runs as homebrew on consoles, in the same online games as everyone else. Most are test builds for now.

Console
Get it

Original Xbox
warthog-xbox, test builds

Xbox 360
warthog-360, test builds

Wii U
warthog-wiiu, test builds

Nintendo Switch
warthog-switch, by thelinkin3000

PlayStation 3
warthog-ps3, by Mayo1970. Work in progress, no release yet.

Other developers have ported it to the PSP, PS Vita, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series (UWP), the Steam Link, and the iPhone, iPad and Apple TV. They play in the same games.

Run a server
The dedicated server runs a playlist of games around the clock. It runs on Linux (x86, x64 or arm64, Raspberry Pi too), on 64-bit Windows, or in Docker, and needs no port forwarding. It can host MCC Workshop maps too. Start with server/README.md.
Builds
Releases are the stable builds, and the game updates itself from them. Want the newest changes early? Pick an update channel in Settings > Online > Updates, or on the setup screen's Updates tab:

Release (the default) gets releases only.
Testing gets test builds first, and may have bugs.
Nightly gets a build of main every night, and the test builds too.

Testing and Nightly still get each release. You can switch back to Release anytime. The game never installs an older build, so after a test build you stay on it until the next release comes out. More in docs/install.md.
Help
Ask on the Discord. It's also where people find games and report bugs. You can file bugs in issues too.
Fixes for common problems, and how to send your logs, are in docs/help.md.
Build it yourself
You need Python 3, ninja and clang. You don't need the Xbox SDK.
python3 configure.py
ninja
Every target and option is in docs/building.md.
Generative AI
The decompilation this project is built on, and the port it began as a fork of, were made with heavy use of generative AI. Chupathingy has its own code and releases now, but a lot of that earlier work is still in it.
We use AI tools the way developers use any other tool. A person decides what to build, reviews every change, tests it, and is responsible for it. Nothing is handed to an AI to build from start to finish without a person involved. We're also working through the code we inherited to clean up what reads as machine-written: comments that only repeat the code, unclear names, and changes nobody can explain.
If you contribute, the same applies to you: see CONTRIBUTING.
License
Chupathingy is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later. It comes with no warranty. Releases up to 0.7.5d stay under CC0. The details, and the permission for console SDKs, are in docs/license.md.
The license covers Chupathingy's code only. It gives no rights in Halo or anything else Microsoft owns.
Support
Chupathingy is free and always will be. Support through
Ko-fi goes to running the site and the servers. If
there's a specific developer or port you'd like to support, ask them: they may
not be part of our community.
Credits

Chupathingy: Milenko and contributors.

Contributors
Fixes from other people's pull requests and forks, taken into Chupathingy
with their authors credited in each commit.

Tyberious: Xbox ADPCM decoding
without the 344 Hz buzz, vertex constant serials that never wrap, pose
snapping for frame interpolation, and the clip-space position kept on the
desktop (no more first-person vertex spikes).
thelinkin3000: the motion sensor for
three and four local players (a split screen crash), and split screen
dividers where the views meet on a wide screen.
xshxdex98 (DamnationCE):
the pause menu's QUIT by mouse or keyboard, and lens flares out of view no
longer tested.
zimm3rmann: visibility test slot 0 kept
apart from the scratch query (lens flares sharing a result).
nsafran1217: no hang
where the visibility results buffer cannot be mapped.
saulob: the first menu frame's colors.
natsu-anon: the cursor hidden during play.
lantos1618: no ghosting in the zoom effect
at high resolutions; on macOS, Command-W does not quit and Command-Q asks
twice.
pfista: projectile trails
ready before a weapon's first shot.
JoshRob297: hosts that run their own games
(the dedicated servers) no longer refuse every join after one arrived as a
game ended.
HiIAmMoot (Mootjuh): the Android menus by
touch, and starting a multiplayer game alone (game.start_with_one_player,
first debug.solo_game), now on by default.
oatkrs: crisp windowed rendering and no
audio cut-outs on macOS, and a corrupted script thread dropped instead of
halting the game.
Renkoto: the FreeBSD port (port/unix,
ninja freebsd64) and its Delta platform, 13.
JizzyRivers: the iOS port (port/ios),
Custom Edition maps and the Map Browser on the original Xbox, and the
consoles' start-up screens and updates.
startupfoundry and
pastudan (OpenH1): camera shake, particle
streams, change colors and camo smoothed between ticks, a faster audio
resampler and limiter, a lighter scope zoom at high resolutions, and a
map's first frame drawn through every shader, which lists the stock maps'
shaders and makes bgfx's pipelines before play.
chestahh (GulchCE): lens flares and light
glows back on AMD graphics, less stutter the first time a texture is drawn
on Windows, host cheat and shadow setup fixes, and the Halo MCC map
loader: MCC Workshop and MCC install maps, their scripts, HUDs, effects
and campaigns.
PeterRichardsonGolf and the other GulchCE contributors: the Steam
Workshop catalog with its items' titles and collections, and the MCC
sharing rules.
mOTA-lEV (OpenCE-Faber):
projectiles and damage that forget objects deleted under them.
bitmoda (mastercheese's OpenCE fork): the
clock read only when something needs it.
theLlamaNet: the Android on-screen touch
controls, through JoshRob297's halo-ce-touch.
Guven (GuvenHuso) and hispanorum (OpenCE): the debug camera flown by
mouse and keyboard, and its saved spot kept for the player in view
(written from a description of their work).

Fonts: Cyborg Interface Gothic, the font of the game's text and of our
own screens, by fizzy, made to match Halo's interface font from Overpass
and glyphs of their own (SIL OFL); the menus' titles in Chupathingy
Titles, Newtown by Roger White (public domain), respaced to sit where
Halo's titles do (SIL OFL);
Overpass (SIL OFL);
Noto Sans (SIL OFL), for the letters
Cyborg lacks, and
Kenney's Input Prompts (CC0); the
scoreboard's platform logos are one-color marks from
Simple Icons (CC0) and Wikimedia Commons (public
domain), plus our own Xbox 360 ring and Wii U GamePad; the names and logos
are their owners' trademarks, used only to identify platforms. The same
marks make the platform badges at the top of this page. BSD Daemon used with permission.
The service record is our own (on the site since September, and in the
Delta Guide's SERVICE RECORD). The Guide's local career totals and top
medals (port/linux/src/service_record.c) follow the career record in
mOTA-lEV's OpenCE-Faber,
used under GPL-3.0 with his permission.
Controller button icons by snapchipper, CC0 (port/assets/prompts).
The Xbox's 3D sound and reverb (audio.hrtf, audio.reverb): the HRTF
measured on an Xbox and the reconstruction of its DSP reverb are
OpenH1's work, brought into
GulchCE by chestahh
(port/linux/src/dsound_xbox_*,
docs/reading/xbox_audio.md).
High-res HUD art on the Xbox maps: Aerocatia's and Jessie's HUD art from
Halo PC Restored (release
r220), used with Aerocatia's permission on the condition that both are
credited; port/assets/hud/NOTICE.md lists which files are theirs.
HD HUDs on Custom Edition maps (MCC's "0.5 HUD scale" and Chimera's
"force HUD use high resolution scale" flags): ugoboom, tested with
Aerocatia's halopc-restored
resource maps.
Stubbs mode reads Stubbs the Zombie's maps with layouts from Sigmmma's
reclaimer (GPL-3.0). The maps
aren't included.
Grifball courts: Bomb plays on SlappyThePirate's "Grifball Beta" court
(grifball.map), which is open to use with credit; the map is not
included.
HaloMD map names: from MacGamingMods' public
HaloMD mod list, so the menus can show each map's own name.
Missing Custom Edition maps: downloaded from the community map
repositories, as Chimera uses them (maps.halonet.net, the HAC2 map
repository, and its mirrors). Chupathingy's downloader is its own code;
Chimera showed where the repositories are and how they answer.
Chimera by SnowyMouse and
contributors (GPL-3.0): Halo PC fixes reference and the compressed map
format.
Security reports: nickarcade, who reported the dedicated server's control
panel permission gap fixed in #462.
Libraries: SDL3, stb, Mbed TLS, miniupnpc, KCP, tomlc17, musl's maths,
Expat, Monocypher, zlib, Zstandard (BSD-3-Clause), the LZMA SDK's decoder
(Igor Pavlov, public domain), SMAA, and Project Nayuki's QR Code generator
(MIT). Their licenses are
beside them in port/third_party. The 64-bit desktop builds' test
renderer uses bgfx, bx and bimg by Branimir Karadžić (BSD-2-Clause), with
glslang and SPIRV-Cross (Khronos, BSD-3-Clause and Apache-2.0), fetched
at build time (tools/bgfx_build.py). Every download carries their notices
and full license texts in one file, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt.

Findings and testing

Sabriel and ugoboom: the Halo PC map reports and regression lists behind
most of the Custom Edition fixes.
Sabriel, roundzabout and Mega: Grifball playtesting and the bugs and
tweaks it turned up.

Where it came from
Chupathingy is a port of the Halo: Combat Evolved decompilation (punpckhdq/halo and bnunu/halo-1). It began as a fork of OpenCE, an earlier port of that decompilation (the code is theirs up to October 9, 2026), and has had its own code, releases and community since.

The decompilation: punpckhdq/halo and
bnunu/halo-1, of the Xbox build 2342.
The port Chupathingy began as a fork of: OpenCE and its contributors, up to
October 9, 2026.
Later fixes taken from OpenCE (CC0), with their authors kept in the

5v76iq.title: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
5v76iq.content: We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2. Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API. Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.What is a decision model?A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:Yes / No: binary decisions.Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels.Score: ordered levels.Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content.Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format. TrainingTurning a generative LLM into a decision modelWe build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions. For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the model’s prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the question’s answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as “location” or an instruction such as “Extract the city name where the job is located.” The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list. Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both waysOur models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backbone’s full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.Training recipeTraining proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backbone’s general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacher’s output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.Adding the ability to extract informationThe locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider. We initialize <|locate|> ’s embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.The span head uses <|locate|> ’s representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> token’s representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the model’s outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.EvaluationWe evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AI’s ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index. Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites. Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Decider’s real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.Query classificationAt Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.Domain-specific classificationWe assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision models’ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).For example, “judge the time complexity of a Python program”, or “use an annual financial report to determine whether a company’s unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve months”. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains. Retrieval and RerankingSearch is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our models’ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each query–document pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points. On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.Multilingual classification To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.NER, PII and Extractive QAWe evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as “person” or “email address”, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflare’s Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each task’s primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category. Image classificationDecider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.Real-world decision requestsWe sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each model’s agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an “Other” category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.Decider ran locally; GLM and DeepSeek used llm-api; Jev used OpenRouter. Reported costs are workload-specific, with unspecified local hardware-cost accounting and no matched latency comparison.RobustnessWe evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each question’s meaning, then checked whether the model’s semantic answer

5hyyfx.title: AMD неожиданно потеряла позиции на рынке настольных процессоров: доля Intel снова превысила 70 %
5hyyfx.content:
Опрос

3DNews Технологии и рынок IT. Новости процессоры AMD неожиданно потеряла позиции на рынке...

реклама

Новости Hardware

Самое интересное в обзорах

13.11.2026 [22:19], 

Intel заметно укрепила позиции на рынке настольных процессоров по итогам третьего квартала 2026 года. Ее доля выросла примерно до 70 %, тогда как AMD впервые за несколько кварталов вновь опустилась ниже 30 %, следует из данных исследовательской компании Mercury Research.
Источник изображения: Intel

Согласно статистике, которую приводит PC Gamer, доля AMD в поставках настольных x86-процессоров сократилась с 34,9 % во втором квартале до 29,9 % в третьем. Соответственно, Intel увеличила присутствие с 65,1 до 70,1 %. Аналитики оценивают изменение примерно в пять процентных пунктов — неожиданный результат после продолжительного укрепления позиций AMD.
Аналитики Mercury Research пока не могут однозначно объяснить причины такого разворота. По одной из версий, сокращение спроса на мобильные процессоры позволило Intel направить больше продукции в настольный сегмент. Ранее компания испытывала трудности с поставками чипов для ПК, а третий квартал традиционно сопровождается сезонным увеличением заказов со стороны производителей компьютеров.

Другим фактором аналитики называют зависимость AMD от игрового рынка. Компания предлагает одни из наиболее производительных игровых процессоров, однако спрос на новые игровые ПК сдерживают дефицит видеокарт и высокие цены на комплектующие. В результате сокращение покупок дорогих игровых систем могло сильнее отразиться на поставках AMD, чем Intel, которая сохраняет значительное присутствие в готовых компьютерах массового сегмента.
Еще во втором квартале AMD увеличила свою долю на рынке клиентских x86-процессоров до рекордных 30,3 %, укрепив позиции как в настольном, так и в мобильном сегментах. При этом рынок настольных CPU уже испытывал серьезные трудности: объем их поставок сократился более чем на 20 % по сравнению с аналогичным периодом предыдущего года.

Новые показатели отражают распределение поставок процессоров между производителями, а не предпочтения покупателей при самостоятельной сборке компьютеров. Поэтому увеличение доли Intel не обязательно свидетельствует о росте популярности ее процессоров среди геймеров. Mercury Research рассматривает изменение структуры поставок и слабый спрос на игровые ПК как возможные причины произошедшего.

j0h78f.title: Sony создала систему передачи запаха из рекламы на билбордах в салон машины
j0h78f.content: Sony оформила патент на любопытную систему – трансляцию запахов из рекламы прямо в салон автомобиля. Заявку подали в США, а опубликовало ее Управление по патентам и товарным знакам США (USPTO). Работает это так: наружная камера распознает рекламный щит, затем система сверяется с онлайн-базой, где для каждой кампании прописан свой аромат, а GPS подтверждает, что машина действительно проезжает мимо нужного места. После этого диспенсеры выпускают в салон соответствующий запах.Как автомобиль распознает рекламуПричем аромат может достаться не всем пассажирам, а выборочно. Внутренняя камера анализирует людей в салоне, в том числе определяет их предполагаемый возраст и пол. Рекламодатель заранее задает условия: например, ограничивает подачу запаха определенной аудиторией или устанавливает длительность в 30 секунд. Технология задумана и для рекламных роликов на телевидении, радио и подключенных устройствах – смартфонах в том числе. В таком случае автомобиль определяет рекламу по телеканалу, сайту или времени трансляции и подбирает подходящий аромат из базы.Реализация и сценарии примененияДля воплощения Sony предлагает использовать ароматические картриджи и вентиляторы, которые направляют запах к отдельным сиденьям.Есть и сценарии вне рекламы. Например, машина может выпускать фирменный аромат при запуске или предлагать пассажирам такси выбрать запах.Правда, получение патента еще не значит, что Sony собирается запускать систему в серийное производство. Ранее, между прочим, Deepal запатентовал ванночку для мытья ног в автомобиле.О другом необычном устройстве для автомобиля «За рулем» уже подробно рассказывал.Понравилась публикация?Тогда добавьте «За рулем» в список интересных источников: 1. Откройте https://google.com... 2. Поставьте галочку напротив нашего изданияГотово – остаемся на связи! «За рулем» можно читать и в MAX

gh-1442191199.title: GitHub - lagando/MKSM: Static recompilation of Mortal Kombat: Shaolin Monks (PS2) to native PC code with PS2Recomp. Vulkan GS renderer, VU1 JIT. No game data included: bring your own copy.
gh-1442191199.content:
English · Português (Brasil)
A static recompilation of Mortal Kombat: Shaolin Monks for PlayStation 2 (USA, SLUS-210.87) to native PC code, built on PS2Recomp.
This is not an emulator and not a remaster. The game's MIPS code (its ELF) is translated to C++ and compiled as a native program. The hardware that is not the CPU (GS, VU, DMA, IOP, SPU2) is still emulated by the PS2Recomp runtime, with our own changes on top.

This repository contains no game data. No ISO, ELF, generated code, recordings or assets, and it does not help you get them. You need your own copy of the game.

Status

Area
State

Recompile the ELF (13,651 C++ files) and build the runtime
✅ Done

Boot, threads, disc reads (CRI ADXF / GAMEDATA.WAD)
✅ Done

Save screens, main menu, character select
✅ Done

First 3D stage (Goro's Lair) with HUD, pause and map
✅ Done

Music and voices (ADX)
✅ Working

GS on the GPU (Vulkan: compute + exact rasterizer with pixel interlock)
✅ Working, bit-exact with the CPU renderer

VU1 on its own thread, x86-64 JIT
✅ Working

Full speed in gameplay (60 fields/s)
✅ 60 on a GTX 1050; heavy scenes drop frames instead of going into slow motion

✅ Intro and all 8 movies play; Start skips

✅ Working (files in extraido_full/mc0/)

✅ 48 kHz without warble; SPU2 reverb still missing

Kung Lao as partner
✅ Visible (used to be invisible)

Every other stage tested start to finish
